title: A practical guide to proper estimation and inference of the Gini index by avoiding often encountered methodological pitfalls
authors: J.F. Muñoz, J.M. Pavía and E. Álvarez-Verdejo
question: The Gini index is the most used measure of inequality. But computing it from data is error-prone. Do common practices give wrong numbers and wrong margins of error?
how: Reviews the many formulas used to compute the Gini index
Tests common methodological pitfalls in large simulation studies
Compares ways of estimating its margin of error
findings: Some widely used formulas give inaccurate estimates of inequality
A popular regression-based method seriously underestimates the margin of error when incomes are very skewed and unequal
Jackknife methods give the most accurate margins of error
why: Margins of error that are too small can make us believe inequality changed when it did not. The paper gives practical recommendations and the free R package giniVarCI.

title: Exploring and correcting the bias in the estimation of the Gini measure of inequality
authors: J.F. Muñoz, P.J. Moya-Fernández and E. Álvarez-Verdejo
question: There are many formulas to estimate the Gini index from a sample. Do they all give the right answer?
how: Classifies the most common estimators of the Gini index
Monte Carlo simulations in a wide range of scenarios
Applications to real data sets
findings: One popular formula strongly overestimates inequality when inequality is low
With skewed and unequal data, the usual estimators tend to underestimate inequality
Bootstrap and jackknife corrections reduce the bias, and a simple criterion tells when to use them
why: Differences in inequality between countries, regions or groups can come from the formula used, not from real differences. Choosing the right estimator avoids wrong conclusions.

title: Does tourism reduce socio-economic inequality? Insights from the pandemic based on space and time models for the EU
authors: C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo
question: Does tourism help to reduce poverty and social exclusion in European regions?
how: EU regions, including the COVID-19 pandemic
Rate of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE)
Spatial models: destinations and neighbouring regions
findings: International (inbound) tourism increases poverty and social exclusion in destination regions
Domestic tourism reduces them, in destinations and in neighbouring regions
Some other effects are statistically significant but economically very small
why: Tourism does not reduce poverty by itself. Market structures, labour regulation, competitiveness and social protection decide who benefits.

title: The “Happy and Poor” paradox: why do some poor people report being very happy?
journal: Applied Research in Quality of Life
authors: J. Guardiola, F. García-Quero and A. García-García
question: Many people living in poverty say they are very happy. How can that be?
how: Systematic review of 40 studies
Evidence mainly from the Global South
Different measures of happiness and poverty
findings: Their basic needs are met and they are satisfied in key areas of life; they adapt to hardship and have modest aspirations
Scientists and policymakers may misjudge how well they are doing
Their culture supports happiness, and maldevelopment has not eroded it
why: Poverty is not only a lack of income. Listening to how people evaluate their own lives helps design better development policies.

title: Does economic growth drive equitable water and sanitation access? Assessing inequality reduction across 64 nations
authors: M. García-López, S. López-Ruiz and G. Cuadrado-Quesada
question: When a country grows richer, does access to water and sanitation become more equal?
how: 64 countries, about 13.5 years each
Data by income quintile and by rural and urban areas
Regression models (OLS, 2SLS and SUR)
findings: Growth improves access overall, but the poorest and rural populations are left behind
Inequality in sanitation is not related to growth
Unequal access to water also holds back GDP per capita
why: Growth alone will not deliver water and sanitation for all (SDG 6). Effective governance and efficient water use are needed.

title: Dynamic spatio-temporal modelling of tourism impact on income inequality and polarization: inbound and domestic flows in the EU
authors: C.M. Llorca-Rodríguez, A.C. Casas-Jurado, R.M. García-Fernández and J. Chica-Olmo
question: Does tourism make income more equal in European regions, or less?
how: EU regions over time
International (inbound) versus domestic tourism
Spatial models: destinations and their neighbours
findings: Overall, tourism and inequality follow an inverted-U shape
Inbound tourism increases inequality and polarization in destinations; domestic tourism reduces them
Both types improve the income distribution of neighbouring regions
why: Useful for the EU Cohesion Policy: domestic tourism supports cohesion, and social protection (education, health, unemployment and retirement) should be strengthened.

title: Inequalities in talents’ earnings: a tale of two European countries
question: Are young graduates paid differently in Italy and in Germany? And are women paid less than men?
how: Graduates aged 25 to 40
EU-SILC data for 2012 and 2022
Wage gaps across the whole wage distribution
findings: The wage gap against Italian talents grew in 2022, mainly because the same qualifications are paid less
The gap grew more for women, especially at the top
Gender gap among talents: Italy from 10% to 22.5%; Germany from 27.5% to 15%
why: Better pay and conditions in Germany help explain why young Italian talents move there. Policies are needed to attract and keep talent.

title: Innovation and poverty-related income gaps in Europe: evidence from the North–South divide
authors: P.A. Cano-Chica, V.E. Yáñez-Justicia, A. Rodríguez-Copete, E. Álvarez-Verdejo and A.J. López-Montoya
question: How are innovation and entrepreneurship related to the income gaps that affect the poorest households in Europe?
how: Eurostat and Global Entrepreneurship Monitor data
Inequality measured by the S80/S20 ratio
Fixed-effects panel and Bayesian hierarchical models
findings: How innovation dynamics interact with income inequality and poverty-related vulnerability
Differences between Northern and Southern Europe
Changes within countries over time and differences between countries
why: Innovation policies can widen or narrow income gaps. Knowing where and how helps to design fairer innovation policies in Europe.
